all.name: Operable (WCAG POUR)
all.statement: UI components and navigation must be operable. All functionality available from keyboard; users have enough time; no seizure-inducing content; navigable and input-modality agnostic.

all.name: Perceivable (WCAG POUR)
all.statement: Information and UI components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. Provide text alternatives for non-text content; captions; content can be presented in different ways.
all.keywords: accessibility perceivable alt text senses w3c

all.name: Robust (WCAG POUR)
all.statement: Content must be robust enough for reliable interpretation by assistive technologies and across user agents. Use valid markup and well-adopted standards.
all.keywords: accessibility robust compatible assistive tech w3c

all.name: This Is for Everyone (GOV.UK)
all.statement: Design inclusively and accessibly for all users. Include those who find services hardest to use; accessibility is not optional.

all.name: Understandable (WCAG POUR)
all.statement: Information and operation of the UI must be understandable. Readable text; predictable behavior; input assistance and error identification/suggestion.

all.name: Do the Hard Work to Make It Simple (GOV.UK)
all.statement: Simplicity requires effort. Take complexity out of the system so that the user experience is simple especially when the underlying systems are complex.

all.name: Occam's Razor
all.statement: Among competing hypotheses the simplest solution is usually the best. Prefer minimal UI.

all.name: Tesler's Law (Conservation of Complexity)
all.statement: For any system there is a certain amount of complexity that cannot be reduced. It can only be moved.

all.name: Choice Overload
all.statement: When people are given too many options they can become overwhelmed and find it harder to make a decision. Reduce options or chunk and guide.

all.name: Consistency and Standards (Nielsen)
all.statement: Users should not wonder whether different words situations or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.

all.name: Doherty Threshold
all.statement: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace under 400ms so neither has to wait on the other.

all.name: Error Prevention (Nielsen)
all.statement: Prevent problems before they occur. Eliminate error-prone conditions or check for them; confirm before destructive or irreversible actions.

all.name: Fitts's Law
all.statement: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target. Larger closer elements are selected more quickly.
all.keywords: target size distance tap click touch

all.name: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use (Nielsen)
all.statement: Accelerators for expert users may speed up interaction. Allow users to tailor frequent actions. Cater to both inexperienced and experienced users.

all.name: Help Users Recognize Diagnose Recover from Errors (Nielsen)
all.statement: Error messages should be expressed in plain language; indicate the problem; and suggest a constructive solution. Avoid error codes only.
all.keywords: error message plain language solution heuristic

all.name: Help and Documentation (Nielsen)
all.statement: Provide help and documentation when needed. Easy to search; focused on the user's task; list concrete steps; and not too large.

all.name: Hick's Law
all.statement: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices. Too many options overwhelm users.

all.name: Jakob's Law
all.statement: Users spend most of their time on other sites and prefer your site to work the same way as sites they already know. Familiarity enhances UX.

all.name: Match System and Real World (Nielsen)
all.statement: Use language and concepts familiar to the user. Follow real-world conventions; information appears in natural order. Metaphors from everyday life.

all.name: Material Motion Responsive
all.statement: Motion reacts quickly to user input (150–400ms). Feedback and transitions feel immediate and natural.

all.name: Minimum Touch Target (Apple HIG)
all.statement: On touchscreen interactive elements need a hit target of at least 44×44 points to accommodate a fingertip. Include padding so controls are distinguishable.

all.name: Motion Provides Meaning
all.statement: Motion respects the user as prime mover. Transitions are meaningful efficient coherent. Responsive 150–400ms; natural (gravity/friction); aware; intentional.

all.name: Paradox of the Active User
all.statement: Users prefer to do rather than read or learn. They start using before mastering; design for immediate use and progressive disclosure.
all.keywords: active user learn by doing documentation

all.name: Postel's Law (Robustness)
all.statement: Be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you send. Tolerate varied input; output consistently.

all.name: User Control and Freedom (Nielsen)
all.statement: Users often choose system functions by mistake. Support undo and redo; provide a clear emergency exit; allow reversal of actions.

all.name: Visibility of System Status (Nielsen)
all.statement: Keep users informed about what is going on through appropriate feedback within a reasonable time. System status and progress should be visible.

all.name: Chunking
all.statement: Group related information into small meaningful units (about 4-7 items) to aid memory and scanning.

all.name: Cognitive Load
all.statement: The amount of mental resources needed to understand and interact with an interface. Minimize unnecessary load.

all.name: Miller's Law
all.statement: The average person can only keep 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory.

all.name: Recognition Rather Than Recall (Nielsen)
all.statement: Minimize the user's memory load. Make objects actions and options visible. User should not have to remember information from one part of the dialogue to another.

all.name: Serial Position Effect
all.statement: Users best remember the first and last items in a list. Primacy and recency.
all.keywords: first last list order primacy recency

all.name: Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)
all.statement: Items that stand out are more likely to be remembered.

all.name: Zeigarnik Effect
all.statement: People remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones.

all.name: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design (Nielsen)
all.statement: Dialogues should not contain irrelevant or rarely needed information. Every extra unit of information competes with relevant units and diminishes their visibility.

all.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
all.statement: Users perceive aesthetically pleasing design as more usable.

all.name: Bold Graphic Intentional
all.statement: Print-based design—typography grids space scale color imagery—creates hierarchy meaning and focus. Bold graphic choices immerse users.
all.keywords: typography grid scale color hierarchy android

all.name: Flow (Csikszentmihalyi)
all.statement: A state of focused engagement where the user is fully immersed. Design for clear goals immediate feedback and matched challenge to skill.

all.name: Goal-Gradient Effect
all.statement: People are more motivated as they get closer to a goal. Progress indicators increase completion.

all.name: Law of Common Region (Gestalt)
all.statement: Elements sharing a clearly defined boundary are perceived as groups.

all.name: Law of Proximity (Gestalt)
all.statement: Objects near each other tend to be grouped together.

all.name: Law of Prägnanz (Gestalt)
all.statement: People perceive ambiguous images as the simplest form possible.

all.name: Law of Similarity (Gestalt)
all.statement: Similar elements are perceived as a complete group.

all.name: Law of Uniform Connectedness (Gestalt)
all.statement: Elements that are visually connected (e.g. by line or color) are perceived as more related than elements with no connection.

all.name: Mental Model
all.statement: Users form a mental model of how the system works. Design so that the system model matches the user's mental model to reduce errors and confusion.

all.name: Peak-End Rule
all.statement: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end rather than the total sum of every moment.

all.name: Adaptivity (Apple HIG)
all.statement: Interfaces adapt to different devices orientations and screen sizes. Maintain focus on content; use visual weight for importance; support portrait and landscape.

all.name: Be Consistent Not Uniform (GOV.UK)
all.statement: Use common patterns and language while allowing flexibility for different circumstances. Consistency helps users; uniformity can constrain.

all.name: Clarity (Apple HIG)
all.statement: Interfaces should be easily understood so users can navigate and interact without confusion. Text is legible; icons are precise; functionality is obvious.

all.name: Consistency (Apple HIG)
all.statement: Maintain familiar patterns across Apple platforms. Standard controls and paradigms reduce cognitive load and match user expectations.

all.name: Deference (Apple HIG)
all.statement: Focus on content over UI chrome. Content takes center stage; interface recedes. Fluidity and deference to user control.
all.keywords: content first chrome minimal ios apple

all.name: Depth (Apple HIG)
all.statement: Use visual layers and motion to communicate hierarchy and organization. Depth and fluid motion connect interface elements and clarify structure.
all.keywords: depth hierarchy layers motion ios apple

all.name: Material is the Metaphor
all.statement: Surfaces and edges provide visual cues grounded in tactile reality (paper and ink). Light surface and movement convey how objects interact in space.
all.keywords: material surface paper ink android metaphor

all.name: Design Based on Understanding (ISO 9241-210)
all.statement: Design is based on an explicit understanding of users tasks and environments. Design decisions are grounded in who will use the system and in what context.
all.keywords: human-centred design context tasks users iso

all.name: Evaluation-Driven Design (ISO 9241-210)
all.statement: Design is driven and refined by user-centred evaluation. The design is validated and improved through testing and feedback with users.

all.name: Iterate. Then Iterate Again (GOV.UK)
all.statement: Release minimum viable products early; test with users; and continuously refine. Iteration reduces risk and improves outcomes.

all.name: Iterative Design (ISO 9241-210)
all.statement: The design process is iterative. Progress through repeated cycles of refinement based on evaluation results.

all.name: Multidisciplinary Team (ISO 9241-210)
all.statement: The design team includes diverse skills and perspectives necessary to address human factors and system requirements.

all.name: Start with User Needs (GOV.UK)
all.statement: Research and understand what users actually need. Do not make assumptions; start with user needs not government or technology constraints.

all.name: User Involvement (ISO 9241-210)
all.statement: Users are involved throughout design and development. Active participation across all stages of the design process.

all.name: Whole User Experience (ISO 9241-210)
all.statement: Design addresses the whole user experience. Consider all aspects of how users interact with and experience the system.
